title: Verbs That Misbehave
tagline: Why English verbs have such strange pasts, and how to learn them in families with a story each, not one by one.
card: A verb that borrowed its past from another verb, and a way to learn the twenty most common irregular verbs in five small stories.
goal: you will see why English has irregular verbs, learn them in sound families, and keep each family in one short story or one room.

story.heading: The verb that borrowed a past

text: Every learner of English eventually asks the same question: why? Why is the past of walk simply walked, but the past of go is went, which has nothing to do with go? Why is it sing, sang, sung but bring, brought, brought? It looks like chaos, and a learner who tries to memorise each verb separately may feel it is.

The answer is old, and it is interesting. Long before English was English, the Germanic languages made the past tense of many verbs by changing the vowel: sing, sang. That was the normal way. Later a new, simpler way arrived: just add -ed. It spread to almost every new verb, and the old vowel-changing verbs became the exceptions we call irregular.

check.q: Why are some English verbs irregular?
check.a: They are survivors of an older system in which the past was made by changing the vowel. The simpler -ed ending later took over almost every other verb.

parts.talk: Which English irregular verb gave you the most trouble? What did you do about it?

text: A few verbs have an even stranger history. Go once had its own past, but it was lost, and English borrowed the past of another verb, wend, which meant 'to travel'. Wend got a new regular past, wended, and its old past, went, was left over. So the past of go is the past of a different verb.
And be is made up of at least three different old verbs wearing one coat: be, been come from one; am, is, are from another; was, were from a third. That is why they look nothing like each other.

check.q: Where does the past tense 'went' come from?
check.a: From the verb 'wend' (to travel): English borrowed its old past for 'go'.

parts.talk: Does it help to know the history? Or do you just want a method for learning them?

text: The good news is that the chaos has a pattern. Most irregular verbs fall into small families that share a sound. Sing, ring, drink, swim, begin all change their vowel in the same way. Bring, buy, think, teach, catch all end their past in -ought or -aught. If you learn the families, you learn dozens of verbs at once.
And a family is exactly the kind of thing a memory method likes: a small group, with a shared sound, that can be held in one picture or one room. That is what you will do in this lesson.

check.q: How can irregular verbs be learned more easily?
check.a: In families that share a sound pattern, each held in one story or one picture.

parts.talk: Which verbs in your language change in strange ways? Are they also in families?

words.m: not following the usual rule. An irregular verb.
the form used after have: sung, brought, gone.
a repeated arrangement. The verbs follow a pattern.
here: a group of verbs that behave in the same way.
an old word meaning to go or to travel.
something that does not follow the rule.

source: The history of went (from wend) and of the verb be is standard in dictionaries of English. Told here in our own words.

method.x: Do not learn twenty verbs. Learn five families and a story for each.

head: Family
Pattern
Verbs (infinitive, past, past participle)
rows: sing, sang, sung · ring, rang, rung · drink, drank, drunk · swim, swam, swum · begin, began, begun · sink, sank, sunk
the past ends in -ought or -aught, same as the participle
bring, brought · buy, bought · think, thought · seek, sought · fight, fought · catch, caught · teach, taught

method.title: Family 1: I-A-U
lines: I → A → U: the vowel goes i, a, u.

Every morning I SING; yesterday a swimmer SWAM across the lake while a bell RANG, a thirsty fish DRANK from it and SANK, and then a choir BEGAN to sing. Today the swimmer has SWUM, the bell has RUNG, the fish has DRUNK and has SUNK, and the choir has SUNG.
method.pic: A swimmer, a bell, a sinking fish and a choir, all in one lake: i, a, u.

method.title: Family 2: -ought and -aught
method.given: bring, buy, think, seek, fight, catch, teach.
lines: The past and the participle are the same, and end in -ought or -aught.
A fisherman BOUGHT a boat and BROUGHT it home. He THOUGHT he would CATCH a whale, so he SOUGHT one at sea. He CAUGHT a small fish, FOUGHT it for an hour, and TAUGHT his son to do the same.
method.pic: One fisherman, one boat, one whale that got away, one small fish.

method.x: For the other three families, make your own stories. Or give each family a room: the I-A-U verbs in the kitchen, the -ought verbs in the hall. The method is the same as for any list: a picture or a story, and a place.
Say the past and the participle for sing, bring, know and go, then say your story for family 1 aloud.

try.title: Which family?
try.prompt: Match each verb to its family.

try.title: A story for family 4
try.prompt: Write a short story that uses know, grow, throw, fly, draw in the past (knew, grew, threw, flew, drew) and again in the past participle (known, grown, thrown, flown, drawn).
try.model: I knew a boy who grew an enormous cabbage, and threw it into the sky. It flew over the town and he drew a picture of it. Today the cabbage has grown a hundred leaves, and people have known him all his life; it has been thrown, flown and drawn a thousand times.
checks: Each is in the past and in the participle.
The story is one strange scene.

try.why: After 'has' we use the past participle: sung.

try.title: Tell the family
try.prompt: Tell your family 2 fisherman story aloud, then say all seven verbs in three forms (bring, brought, brought...).

quiz.q: What is the past participle of 'drink'?

quiz.why: 'Went' is the old past of 'wend', borrowed for 'go'.

opts: One story holds several verbs with the same sound pattern
quiz.why: A family shares a pattern, so one story or one room holds many.
